blocks.text: Backtracking explores alternatives and greedy methods commit when a structural argument permits commitment. Dynamic programming takes another route: identify subproblems whose answers recur, compute each relevant answer once, and combine those answers according to a recurrence. blocks.text: To justify optimal substructure, take an optimal nonempty combination and remove one chosen coin c. If its remainder were not optimally solved, replacing that remainder by a better solution would improve the original combination, contradicting optimality. Conversely, every candidate is feasible because it adds a valid coin to a feasible remainder.

blocks.text: The state must preserve every constraint affecting future choices. If only one coin of each physical item may be used, remaining amount alone is insufficient because two paths can leave different inventories. A state might then include the next available item index or a bounded inventory description. Reusing the unbounded-coin recurrence would silently allow spending an item more than once.

blocks.text: Optimal substructure is not permission to take the largest denomination greedily. For denominations one, three, and four, amount six is best represented by two threes. Taking four first leaves two ones and uses three coins. Dynamic programming considers each valid last choice and compares the resulting totals rather than assuming that the locally largest coin must belong to an optimum.

blocks.text: The proof also identifies what a reconstruction witness must satisfy. A reported count is not enough: the returned coins must all be allowed denominations, sum exactly to the target, and have length equal to the count. Optimality then needs the recurrence argument or an independent oracle on a bounded domain. These checks diagnose different defects and should remain separate in the test suite.

Rejecting these inputs before recursion is more reliable than hoping the memoization machinery will rescue them.

blocks.text: The usual time bound here is O(A*K) for K denominations, because each of at most A + 1 states considers the denomination collection. It is a bound in the numeric value of the amount, not merely in the number of bits used to encode it. Calling this pseudo-polynomial makes that distinction explicit: doubling the bit length can allow a vastly larger table even though the input representation grew modestly.

Setting a state initially to impossible before its loop is safe here because every recursive dependency has a strictly smaller amount. There is no cycle that can revisit an in-progress state under validated positive denominations. This shortcut would not generalize to an arbitrary cyclic dependency graph.

The maximum accepted amount is five hundred. This deliberately bounds recursion depth, table size, and count arithmetic for the teaching example. Top-down evaluation can avoid states that no denomination path reaches, but its call stack and callable overhead remain real implementation costs. A larger target range may favor the iterative version even when asymptotic bounds agree.

Top-down memoization preserves the recursive shape of the problem. A request for an amount first checks whether the answer is already stored. If not, it asks for smaller reachable amounts, chooses the best result, records it, and returns. Only states reached through these calls are evaluated.

The supplied function requires every denomination to be positive. This is both a domain choice and a termination condition. A zero denomination would recursively request the same amount without progress before its result had been stored. A negative denomination could increase the remaining amount and leave the allocated table. Rejecting these inputs before recursion is more reliable than hoping the memoization machinery will rescue them.

With a denomination of one, a recursive chain can have depth proportional to the target amount. The companion deliberately limits the target to five hundred. That bound keeps the teaching stack depth and table size modest; it is not an assertion that every platform has the same safe recursion limit. A larger application may favor bottom-up iteration even when the recurrence is unchanged.

Failure caching requires care with side effects. This example’s result depends only on fixed denominations and an integer amount. A subproblem that performs a network request or reads changing external state is not made pure merely by putting its return value in a map. Decide which observations can be reused and for how long before applying memoization outside a mathematical kernel.

The usual time bound here is O(A*K) for K denominations, because each of at most A + 1 states considers the denomination collection. It is a bound in the numeric value of the amount, not merely in the number of bits used to encode it. Calling this pseudo-polynomial makes that distinction explicit: doubling the bit length can allow a vastly larger table even though the input representation grew modestly.

blocks.text: A valid witness demonstrates feasibility, not optimality by itself. Agreement between two programs using one recurrence is stronger than one unchecked result but weaker than independent modeling evidence. The professional habit is to combine a clear recurrence, a dependency argument, bounded exhaustive checks, and witnesses that can be validated without trusting the solver’s internal table.
